Tingle ended the working week on 12 January 
by closing the hatches to Dragon, checking 
petri dishes for condensation, and installing an 
instrument for imaging NASA’s Advanced Plant 
Experiments 03-1(APEX-03-1) study, which 
examines the effects of microgravity on the 
development of roots and cells on plant seedlings. 
Acaba, who is of Puerto Rican heritage, spoke to 
students from the Institute of Robotics in San Juan, 
while Misurkin and Shkaplerov took body mass 
measurements using the Space Linear Acceleration 
Mass Measurement Device (SLAMMD), and 
worked on the Russian Biocard cardiovascular 
investigation and the DAN blood pressure study.
DRAGON TAKES FLIGHT
The unmanned Dragon spacecraft was unberthed 
from the Earth-facing side of Harmony at 22:47 
UTC on 12 January by Canadarm2, and released 
by the robotic arm the following day at 09:58 UTC 
as the complex flew 418.4 km above southern 
Australia. This was the first time a Dragon release 
was commanded by ground controllers instead of 
the astronauts aboard the ISS, who monitored the 
manoeuvre from inside the Cupola. 
Dragon performed its de-orbit burn at 14:43 
UTC on 13 January and splashed down in the 
Pacific Ocean at 15:37 UTC (07:37 local time), 625 
km off the coast off Baja, California carrying 1,850 
kg of cargo and experiments. Time-critical items 
were removed from the vehicle and sent to JSC 
within 48 hr of splashdown, once Dragon arrived 
at Long Beach, California. The spacecraft itself was 
then taken to its McGregor, Texas test facility for 
post flight processing. Aside from Dragon’s release, 
the crew enjoyed a light-duty weekend 13/14 
January, performing regular housekeeping chores, 
daily exercising, and talking to family and friends.
The crew began a week of EVA preparations 
on 15 January for their forthcoming respective 
spacewalks. Acaba worked with the RR-6 
experiment, while Kanai focused on ESA’s Biolab 
facility, and Misurkin and Shkaplerov worked 
with the Russian Biocard and Splanh biomedical 
experiments.
The crew operated JAXA’s Microbe-1experiment 
on 16 January, periodically monitoring, collecting 
and analysing samples of fungi and bacteria inside 
Kibo. Acaba conducted further research with the 
RR-6 study, while Kanai continued to work with 
Biolab. Misurkin and Shkaplerov took photos 
of Earth courtesy of the Uragan (Hurricane) 
experiment and investigated the physical 
performance of cosmonauts on long-duration 
missions using the Profilkatika-2 hardware.
Zvezda’s engines were fired for 15.6 sec at 20:15 
UTC on 17 January to place the ISS in a 422.7 x 
402.8 km orbit, necessitated by the arrival and 
departure of the next Progress and Soyuz spacecraft 
respectively. The crew replaced a lamp on the 
Fluids Integrated Rack and returned to NASA’s 
NeuroMapping experiment, which studies changes 
to the brain during long duration missions. Kanai 
worked with ESA’s Circadian Rhythms experiment, 
which examines how an astronaut’s biological clock 
adapts to life in space.
Vande Hei and Tingle conducted an EMU 
fit check on 18 January for their spacewalk and 
configured their EVA tools the following day. The 
crew took images of Southern California as part 
of the ongoing Crew Earth Observation (CEO) 
programme and did research with the Russian 
Matryoshka-R radiation investigation.
On 19 January, the 7,000th day since the launch 
of Zarya, Misurkin and Shkaplerov conducted an 
eye exam using a fundoscope, whilst Vande Hei, 
Tingle and Kanai reviewed spacewalk procedures 
with ground specialists ahead of their EVAs. 
Kanai wrapped up his session with the Circadian 
Rhythms experiment at the start of the crew’s light-
duty weekend 20/21 January.
Vande Hei and Tingle made final preparations 
inside Quest on 22 January for their EVA. The crew 
also did further work with the NeuroMapping and 
the RR-6 experiments and the Russian Cosmocard 
medical study and NASA’s Light Microscopy 
Module (LMM), which enables novel research of 
microscopic phenomena in microgravity.

at 11:49 UTC on 23 January to replace the 190 kg 
degraded Latching End Effector-B (LEE-B) on 
the end of Canadarm2 with a spare – the robotic 
arm now has two fully functional grappling 
mechanisms. However, as the newly installed LEE 
was undergoing tests on 26 January, an anomaly 
was detected in one of the two electronic systems 
that control its mechanisms. 
The following day, Vande Hei and Tingle 
took part in a post-EVA debriefing with ground 
specialists, while other members of the crew 
worked for several days with ESA’s Arthrospira 
biology experiment, the NeuroMapping study, 
and NASA’s ongoing Meteor experiment, which 
examines the chemical composition of meteors 
entering Earth’s atmosphere.
On 25 January, Kanai checked out a 3D-printed 
satellite deployer which will spring-launch four 
tiny satellites, known as FemtoSats, from the 
station. Acaba tended to two science freezers, 
ensuring they maintained the proper temperature 
necessary for storing biological samples, while 
Misurkin and Shkaplerov worked with the Russian 
Pilot-T investigation, which aims to assess how 
cosmonauts perform complicated robotic tasks 
from orbit.
Acaba ended the working week on 26 January 
by installing the plant habitat science carrier into 
the new Advanced Plant Habitat facility – a self-

RUSSIAN RECORD-BREAKERS
Misurkin and Shkaplerov opened Pirs’ hatch to 
begin their EVA at 15:34 UTC on 2 February, 
installing a new electronics and telemetry box 
for the Lira high-gain antenna on Zvezda to 
enhance communications via the Luch satellites 
in geostationary orbit. Misurkin jettisoned the 
old electronics box at 19:40 UTC on a retrograde 
trajectory behind Zvezda’s engines. 
When ground controllers attempted to 
command the antenna to rotate back to its 
operational position, it snagged on equipment 
previously used to help Europe’s Automated 
Transfer Vehicles (ATVs) dock to Zvezda. Misurkin 
and Shkaplerov helped to clear the impediment, 
but when engineers commanded the antenna 
to move, it rotated beyond its normal position.

experiments and performed a photographic survey 
of the exterior of the Russian segment. 
The spacewalk ended at 23:47 UTC after 8 hr 
13 min, making it the longest Russian EVA in 
history – surpassing by 6 min the previous longest, 
conducted in 2013 (SpaceFlight Vol 56 No 3 pages 
96-97). It was also the fifth longest spacewalk in 
history and the 207th dedicated to ISS assembly 
and maintenance totalling 53 days 22 hr 4 min.
On 5 February, Misurkin and Shakplerov stowed 
their Orlan suits and cleaned the Pirs airlock, while 
Tingle and Kanai began several more days of work 
with the RR-6 study and Vande Hei returned to the

Vande Hei set up botany gear inside Columbus 
on 6 February for NASA’s Veggie-3 experiment, 
exploring the feasibility of harvesting edible plants. 
The crew also collected surface and air samples for 
NASA’s Microbial Tracking-2 (MT-2) experiment 
and stored them inside the Minus Eighty-Degree 
Laboratory Freezer for ISS (MELFI) for later 
analysis, while the Russian cosmonauts performed 
a leak check on Progress 68 and worked with the 
Biocard investigation.
On 7 February Acaba and Vande Hei spoke

about their mission and the future of international 
cooperation in space. Misurkin and Shkaplerov 
conducted further eye tests, while Tingle and 
Kanai continued with the RR-6 experiment inside 
Destiny.

It flies. But
where to?
The launch of SpaceX’s Falcon Heavy has rightly created 
much excitement as the most powerful rocket to ﬂy 
since the Saturn V. But claims of its usefulness may be 
greatly exaggerated. The Moon and Mars are off-limits, 
so where is it going – and why?

rocket stages, strapped together and pushing a 
monster payload carrying a team of astronauts 
to Mars. Something which at the time NASA 
envisaged could happen in the 1980s. Apart from 
the more conventional form of propulsion, and the 
fact that it was unmanned, the launch of Falcon 
Heavy was exactly that – except that this time 
in place of a crew there was Elon Musk’s first- 
generation Tesla electric car at the front end! 
We have had electric cars in space before – three 
Lunar Roving Vehicles on each of the last Moon 
landings, as well as Russian and Chinese rovers – 
but this one was going all the way past Mars and on 
towards the Asteroid Belt. That’s serious. As Musk 
himself said: “Sometimes it’s fun to do silly things!” 
And yet, in spite of the deafening background 
screams and whoops of delight threatening to 
overwhelm the launch commentator’s voice, it was 
a serious bid to push the boundaries – to rewrite 
the script and fly in the face of scepticism. 
Was it a stunt? No. Was it a meaningful 
contribution to deep-space exploration? No. 
Why? Because SpaceX has already moved on 
from arguably the most challenging project this 
successful rocket company has ever undertaken –
and the market has moved on, too. Elon Musk has 
already abandoned any idea of putting people on 
Falcon Heavy, of sending it on tourist trips around 
the Moon, or of using it to send people to Mars.

By definition, FH-1 is a Super Heavy launch vehicle 
– a class of rocket capable of lifting in excess of 49 
tonnes to Low Earth Orbit (LEO), of which there 
have been only three to date. It joins the Saturn V 
and Russia’s Energia as the only Super Heavies to 
have successfully sent payloads into space. With

a LEO capacity of 140 tonnes, Saturn V flew 13 
times, supported nine lunar missions, and placed 
the Skylab space station in Earth orbit on its final 
flight in 1973. Energia, which could loft 100 tonnes 
into LEO, flew twice – in 1987 and 1988 – and 
on its second flight successfully placed the Buran 
shuttle in orbit. Falcon Heavy has flown once, but 
may never fly more missions than the Saturn V.  
So what future does it have and how will it sit 
within a fast-encroaching and highly competitive 
heavy-lift launcher market? 
The story really began in 2004, two years after 
the formation of SpaceX. At that time there were 
signs that the communications satellite market 
would support a manifest sufficiently robust to 
justify the development of a heavy lifter. Stimulated 
by the interest of potential customers, Musk 
was ready with several options to achieve that 
capability. Most obvious was to use the existing 
assets focused on getting the Falcon 9 operational 
and to employ legacy technology.
Problems with the Falcon 9 (so named because 
of the nine Merlin rocket motors in the first stage) 
put back plans to focus on the Heavy and this, too, 
delayed a decision on the exact configuration of 
the big rocket. Nevertheless, the first successful 
flight of Falcon 9 on 4 June 2010 – a year before 
the last Shuttle flight – provided fresh impetus and 
encouragement. Clients were already lining up to 
reserve slots on this new commercial venture, and 
when the second Falcon 9 flight sent the Dragon 
capsule into space on 8 December that year, it 
demonstrated a unique and exciting capability. 
Confidence was raised still further when SpaceX 
launched its third Falcon 9 mission on 23 May 
2012, resulting in a Dragon capsule docking with 
the International Space Station – the first company 
under NASA’s Commercial Orbit Transportation 
Services (COTS) programme to deliver cargo to 
the ISS. When the Dragon capsule returned intact 
several days later, it scored yet another “first”, 
successfully surviving re-entry and recovery with 
the potential to return with up to 2,500 kg of cargo. 
Less than one week later, with 40 commercial 
flights booked aboard Falcon 9 rockets, SpaceX 
received a letter of intent from Intelsat for Falcon 
Heavy slots. The definitive design focused on 
the use of three core stages in a parallel burn 
configuration. In their search for the lowest flight 
cost, enabling SpaceX to offer highly competitive 
launch prices, design engineers locked on to the 
most effective way to produce a powerful launch 
vehicle: commonality. 
This approach, which has always driven 
commercial launch providers, started out during 
the early 1960s with the development of the Thor 
into the Delta, making possible a set of production-
line hardware consisting of upper stages, booster 
options and fairing sizes. The SpaceX approach was 
preceded by the Common Booster Core concept 
adopted by Boeing in their Delta IV Heavy variant 
for the US Air Force Evolved Expendable Launch 
Vehicle (EELV) programme. which was capable 
of placing 29 tonnes in Low Earth Orbit (LEO). 
The first flight of a Delta IV-H on 21 December 
2004 failed to deliver its payload into the intended 
orbit. However, the second flight, on 11 November 
2007, achieved its objective by orbiting a DESP-23 
Defense Support Program early-warning satellite.  
To date, nine Delta IV-H launchers have flown, 
including the launch of the first unmanned Orion 
spacecraft on 5 December 2014. But there are 
booked slots for additional flights at the rate of 
one per year through to the end of 2023. Only one, 
NASA’s Parker Solar Probe in July this year, is not a 
listed flight for the National Reconnaissance Office. 
There is certainly a market for heavy-lift rockets, 
but not a big one – a factor that drives up the cost 
of such vehicles and which may limit the market 
for Falcon Heavy. But more on that later.
A QUESTION OF NUMBERS
By 2012, SpaceX was confident that it could strap 
three first-stage cores together and deliver a cost-
effective, parallel-burn rocket while also producing 
a launch vehicle with considerably greater lifting 
capability than the competition. The company 
believed it could achieve a launch cost of around 
10% that of the Delta IV-H, leaving the way clear  
to build an even bigger payload-lifter known as 
Falcon XX. Projected to carry 150 tonnes into LEO, 
the XX would eclipse even the legendary Saturn 
V. However, as design work intensified on Falcon 
Heavy, it became apparent that all was not well.  
Initial performance estimates pegged Falcon 
Heavy at an LEO lift of 53 tonnes – more than

But to achieve such capability the rocket would 
have to be virtually redesigned, literally from the 
ground up. It was not simply a matter of strapping 
the cores together and lighting the blue touchpaper. 
Much of the difficulty had to do with the vibration 
spectra and acoustic waves of the propellant 
combinations and the Merlin motors. (Delta IV-
H, by contrast, uses cryogenic propellants with 
different spectra more sympathetic to clustering.)
Despite initial projections of a flight in 
2013, there was also a question over the near-
simultaneous ignition of 27 Merlin rocket motors, 
which would expose the central core stage to shock 
waves from the outer cores and create a resonant 
operating environment in which the separate 
motors might not synchronise – a notorious 
consequence of the hydrocarbon fuel used by 
Falcon 9 and Falcon Heavy. As a result of these 
mounting technical and engineering difficulties, the 
schedule slipped. At the same time, development of 
the Falcon 9 increased the potential of the single-
stick rocket and its payload capability.
Reusability was key to the SpaceX formula, 
to which end the company unveiled the Falcon 
9 v.1.1 in September 2013 following a two-year 
development period. Along with increased 
propellant density, the arrangement of its nine 
rocket motors was changed from a 3 x 3 square to 
a circular cluster of eight Merlins around a central 
motor in what SpaceX calls an ‘octaweb’. The new 
rocket had 60% more thrust and was 60% heavier. 
The first successful landing of a Falcon 9 first stage 
occurred on 21 December 2015 with the Falcon 9 
v1.2 (Full Thrust or Block 4 version), followed by 
the first relaunch of a previously flown stage on 30 
March 2017, together with recovery of the payload 
fairing – an expensive item to fabricate. 
The convergence of these capabilities – 
improved engine performance and enhanced 
econometrics based on a proven ability to recover 
and reuse rocket stages on a sustained basis – 
underpinned development of the revised Falcon 
Heavy. Nevertheless, the programme was dogged 
by the need for a complete redesign of the side 
cores, a beefed-up thrust structure and significant 
upgrades to the control systems, as well as issues 
with the aerodynamics of the ogive nose area and 
side loads created by the boosters.
With development time being eaten up and the 
first launch date slipping, Elon Musk tried on at 
least three occasions to have the rocket cancelled, 
but was persuaded otherwise on the basis that 
the spectrum of potential mission opportunities 
was still evolving. With certification for carrying 
classified payloads, Falcon 9 competed directly 
with the Atlas and Delta vehicles offered by ULA 
– and at greatly reduced prices from those the 
government had been used to paying. Out of that 
came a unique payload requirement that appeared 
to justify continued development of Falcon Heavy. 
And as a result, the technology required to meet 
the revised requirement was fed back into the 
development programme.

Further technical developments, which converged 
to produce the Falcon 9 Block 5 version, also 
found their way into Falcon Heavy, but it was the 
re-engineered central core that proved the most 
challenging of all. 
As now built, the definitive Falcon Heavy has 
a theoretical payload capability close to 64 tonnes 
on the strength of 27 Merlin D rocket motors 
delivering a lift-off thrust of 22,819 kN, increasing 
to 24,681 kN in the vacuum of space. These thrust 
levels assume full throttle for the central core 
and side cores, but in reality the thrust levels are 
controlled to relieve stress on the central core and 
to reduce maximum aerodynamic pressure on the 
launch vehicle during ascent (Max Q). The central 
core experiences combined side loads of 4,450 kN 
from the two side cores, which it would not see as a 
single-stick rocket.
HANDSOME IS AS HANDSOME DOES  
Where needed, SpaceX employs cutting-edge 
technology and engineering. The core tank walls 
for Falcon 9 and Falcon Heavy are fabricated in 
an aluminium-lithium alloy, as were the External 
Tank (ET) sections for NASA’s Shuttle, using 
the same friction-stir welding techniques as 
those employed by the (then) Martin Marietta 
corporation on the ET. This commonality also 
extends to the second stage, powered by a single 
Merlin 1D. However, simpler technology is 
employed wherever possible, thereby saving costs 
and enhancing reliability. Examples include the 
interstage section, which consists of a carbon-fibre 
aluminium core composite structure, and the side 
booster separation system, which utilises collets 
and pneumatic pushers. 
Equally, not all of the technical innovations 
considered for the rocket made it through to 
the final design. The original plan was to have 
a propellant crossfeed arrangement from the 
side cores to the central core which would have 
exhausted them quicker and hence lightened the 
ascending stack. However in 2016 this was dropped 
in favour of a central core throttle-down shortly 
after launch, followed by a throttle-up only after 
side booster separation.
In the interests of reusability, SpaceX is also 
giving up substantial lift capability by retaining 
sufficient propellant to return and soft-land 
the three core stages. For example, a published 
capability of 26.7 tonnes to geosynchronous 
transfer orbit (GTO) assumes the full use of all 
loaded propellant for orbital insertion, reducing

FH-1 was brought to LC-39A in late December 2017, 
modiﬁcations to the pad having been completed by 
late October. Integrated in a horizontal position 
prior to its elevation to the vertical on 28 December 
for a ﬁt-check, the rocket was lowered and then 
elevated again on 13 January. Fuelling took place 
on 21 January and a static ﬁring test took place at 
12.30 pm local time on 24 January, giving preview 
of what might be expected on launch day. This was 
the most powerful rendering of rocket power 
anywhere since the last Shuttle mission on 8 July 
2011, and the thunder that ripped across the Cape 
that day gave a portent of the excitement to come. 
The 27 Merlin 1D rocket motors ﬁred for only just 
over 10 seconds, held down by restraint arms, but 
in that time provided enough data from which to 
assess the mighty rocket’s readiness for launch.

But these are trade-offs for a launch cost that is 
already considerably lower than that of competing 
launchers – or indeed any that are likely to emerge 
in the next five years.   
It cost SpaceX around $500 million to develop 
Falcon 9 and bring it to Block 5 status. Adopting 
standard government fee/incentives contracts, 
NASA believes that it would have cost it around 
$4 billion to do what Musk has done with Falcon 
9, or $1.7 billion if it had adopted the commercial 
practices SpaceX has employed. Falcon Heavy 
has cost SpaceX in excess of $550 million to 
get it to a first flight – much more than Elon 
Musk anticipated, and the primary reason for 
his persistent attempts to drop it. Even so, there 
was still a perceived market for the rocket, albeit 
a very different market from the one that had 
underpinned initial investment five years ago. And 
the arguments for continuing with Falcon Heavy 
were sound, as we shall see. 
In anticipation of a wide spectrum of payload 
manifests, negotiations with NASA led to the 
establishment of a second Falcon Heavy launch site, 
in addition to LC-39A, at Vandenberg Air Force 
Base, California. This is ideal for launches into 
polar orbit of both civilian and military satellites, 
and supports certain mission requirements that 
are classified and subject to change. There is no 
doubt that military requirements currently offer the 
strongest justification for having brought Falcon 
Heavy to the pad. They are reflected in the very 
structure of its mission profile and in the trajectory 
flown on its first launch.  
Quite when the Falcon Heavy will be certified 
for national security missions depends on several 
variables, not least the confidence in it displayed 
by the US government, and its reliability record. 
A clearly defined list of requirements is contained 
in the Launch Services New Entrant Certification 
Guide published by the Air Force in 2011. This 
emphasises that certification depends not only on 
what the rocket does, but on the depth of technical 
certainty attached to its manufacturing, processing 
and launch support infrastructure. And while 
SpaceX may have completed the evolutionary 
development of the rocket, it has yet to prove that 
it can fulfil its claimed role. In April 2015, the 
company outlined to the Air Force its own schedule 
that it believed would satisfy the certification 
boards. This comprised three successful flights, two 
of which would be consecutive, but assumed an 
initial flight in 2017. It now seems unlikely that the 
two additional flights will take place before the end 
of 2018 at the earliest.
Even before Falcon Heavy was ready to fly, 
Elon Musk had decided that all development 
work on it, as well as Falcon 9, would cease after 
Block 5 was brought to market this year. This put 
paid to an earlier plan to send a Dragon 2 capsule 
on a circumlunar flight carrying two fee-paying 
passengers. According to SpaceX, two unnamed 
individuals had already placed considerable 
deposits for such flight, which would have utilised 
the Dragon 2 spacecraft being developed to support 
crew transport to and from the International Space 
Station (ISS). Dragon 2 is now unlikely to begin 
carrying crew to the ISS before 2019 at the earliest, 
and NASA planning documents anticipate that it 
will take until 2020. 
On the proposed circumlunar flight, the 
spacecraft would have flown, autonomously or 
under mission control, a trajectory that would 
have taken it to an apogee of 500,000 km – about 
100,000 km beyond the Moon – prior to its return 
to Earth. SpaceX has also cancelled plans for a 
Red Dragon spacecraft adapted to support crewed 
flights to Mars. Despite vigorous publicity and 
a dazzled fan-crowd convinced that this could 
happen, it was never likely to occur: human flights 
to Mars would of necessity have to provide more 
volume per astronaut than could be found within 
the confines of a Dragon capsule.

In spite of the delays and the shelved plans, the 
inaugural flight of Falcon Heavy was always going 
to be something special – notwithstanding Elon 
Musk’s tweets on social media that he gave it only 
a 50-50 chance, and would consider the launch a 
success if it did no more than clear the pad.

countdown resumed, with ignition of the 27 Merlin 
engines at 15:45 hr UTC. Live commentary from 
the SpaceX control centre was virtually drowned 
out by the background shouts, screams and cheers 
of ecstatic personnel witnessing the culmination 
of their decade-long commitment to building the 
world’s biggest rocket.
At T-5 sec, FH-1’s engine controller commanded 
the side cores to ignite, followed by the centre core 
two seconds later. With the centre core throttled 
back and the side cores at full thrust, veteran 
launch-watchers saw Falcon Heavy appear to move 
relatively swiftly off the pad and on toward Max Q 
at 66 sec into the flight. Roll and pitch commands 
went in as planned and the side cores ran smooth 
and hot just they had both done once before – one 
to launch the Thaicom 8 satellite in May 2016, the 
other a Dragon flight to the ISS in July of the same 
year. 
At 2 min 33 sec, the side cores separated – a big 
moment of concern that went exactly as planned. 
In what resembled an elegantly choreographed 
ballet, they then flipped over, ready for their boost-

in unison at designated Landing Zones 1 and 2, 
approximately 7 min 58 sec into the mission. There 
was no such luck for the centre core, which failed 
to make its deceleration burn and crashed into the 
sea 100 m from the shipboard landing platform. 
Back in space, second stage shutdown occurred 
at 8 min 31 sec, marking the start of a 9 min 51 sec

PREFACE 
 
With great pleasure I introduce the report on Space Research in India, 
prepared for the 44th COSPAR Scientific Assembly, 16 – 24 July 2022, 
Athens, Greece, by the Indian National Committee for Space 
Research (INCOSPAR), Indian National Science Academy (INSA), and 
Indian Space Research Organisation (ISRO). The report gives an 
overview of the important accomplishments, achievements and 
research activities conducted in India in several areas of near-Earth 
Space, Sun, Planetary Science, and Astrophysics for the duration of 
one and half years (July 2020 – Dec 2021). This report also provides 
glimpses of capacity building activities in space science research, 
academic courses offered on space science and technology, national 
and international collaborations in space science and technology, 
laboratories and facilities established at various institutes and 
centres contributing to space science exploration and research in 
India, to name a few.  
The Indian space science community has been active in the domains related to Astronomy and 
Astrophysics, Solar Physics, Space Weather and Sun-Earth connection, Space and Atmospheric Sciences, 
Planetary Science, Geomagnetism and Geosciences. This report describes highlights of the research from 
the studies on oceanography, atmospheric structure and dynamics, clouds and convective systems, 
aerosols, radiation and trace gases, weather and climate change, middle atmosphere, ionosphere, 
magnetosphere, solar wind and space weather, lunar and planetary studies, Sun and the solar system 
bodies, stars, galaxies, galactic and extragalactic astronomy and cosmology.  
In the area of planetary science, the Chandrayaan-2 orbiter is providing high-quality remote sensing and 
in-situ observations of the Moon with eight scientific payloads on-board; the data are made available to 
public with more than 2800 worldwide registered users. Chandrayaan-2 science results have provided 
new insights to the lunar science research, which include characterization of hydration features on 
surface, characterization of young, fresh lunar crater floors, global distribution of Argon-40 in the lunar 
exosphere, study of the geotail dynamics at lunar distances, detection of minor elements, such as Cr and 
Mn from the orbiter, and mapping of sodium distribution for the first time.  
The Indian Mars Orbiter Mission (MOM) continues to orbit Mars completing more than seven years of 
operations around Mars. The enhanced escape of Martian atmosphere during global dust storm is one 
of the major science results of MOM.

CHAPTER-1
ORGANISATIONAL STRUCTURE  
AND SCIENCE ACTIVITIES
1.1 INTRODUCTION
The first steps of Indian space science exploration started with the investigations of the 
Earth’s upper atmosphere and ionosphere. The initial scientific motivation was to study 
equatorial electrojets. In the year 1963, the first sounding rocket was launched from the 
Thumba Equatorial Rocket Launching Station (TERLS) near Thiruvananthapuram. These 
sounding rockets were meant to investigate the upper atmospheric regions using rocket-
borne instruments. Sounding rocket launched are conducted periodically from Thumba, a 
place near southern tip of India very close to the Earth magnetic equator. The rocket based 
experiments provided initial opportunities to conduct the scientific investigations of high 
altitudes upper regions of magnetic equator which was not accessible through balloons and 
satellites. Presently more than 3500 rocket launches have been carried out successfully by 
ISRO with national and international participation. The TERLS Range is dedicated to the 
United Nations since 1968 and all member countries of the UN are welcome to use this 
facility  for various scientific research. Presently RH-200, RH-300 Mk-II and RH-560-Mk-III 
sounding rockets are operational with payload capacity ranging from 8 to 100 kg and apogee 
range of 80 to 475 km. Since then, the ISRO has developed the technologies for various 
launch vehicles, satellites and payloads and the Indian Space programme has grown from 
humble beginnings to achieve our vision of utilization of space for societal development. 
The seeds sown more than six decades ago have fructified to yield indigenous capabilities 
to achieve independent access to space along with a plethora of space-based services 
which are transforming India. The space science and exploration missions undertaken 
during the next level of growth of the space programme such as the Chandrayaan-1, Mars 
Orbiter Mission, Astrosat and Chandrayaan-2 missions are yielding valuable scientific data 
and are contributing to the global knowledge base of the cosmos. ISRO is also planning a 
human space flight mission in low earth orbit in near future which will open opportunities for 
microgravity experiments for various cutting edge scientific investigations.
1.2 	 ORGANISATION OF SPACE RESEARCH
	
INDIAN NATIONAL COMMITTEE FOR SPACE RESEARCH 
(INCOSPAR)
Indian National Committee for Space Research (INCOSPAR) is one of the committees of 
the Indian National Science Academy (INSA), which is the national adhering organisation 
to the International Council of Scientific Unions (ICSU), and a member of ICSU Council. 
Presently Dr. Anil Bhardwaj is the Chairman of INCOSPAR and Dr. K Rajeev is the national 
representatives at COSPAR Council. INCOSPAR has the following terms of references.
Space Science Exploration and Research 
in India
2
I.	 To recommend and promote national activities and international co-operation in space 
exploration and space research.
II.	 To provide necessary liaison with the COSPAR of ICSU, and encourage participation in 
international activities which contribute to the peaceful uses of outer space.
1.3 	 SPACE COMMISSION, DEPARTMENT OF SPACE AND 
INDIAN SPACE RESEARCH ORGANISATION
The Space Commission and the Department of Space (DOS) were established by the 
Government of India in 1972 to promote development and application of space science and 
technology for identified national socio-economic objectives. The Space Commission lays 
down the framework of important space activities and advises the Government on major 
policies related to India’s space programme. DOS functions directly under the Prime Minister 
of India. Shri S. Somanath is the present Chairman of the Space Commission, Secretary to 
the Government of India in DOS and Chairman of the Indian Space Research Organisation 
(ISRO). 
The Indian Space Programme is directed towards the goal of self-reliant use of space 
science and technology for national development, its main thrusts being:
I.	 Satellite telecommunications, navigation, television and radio broadcasting
II.	 Satellite remote sensing for resource survey and management, environmental monitoring 
and meteorological services.
III.	Development and operationalization of indigenous satellites and launch vehicles for 
providing these services.
DOS is responsible for carrying out space research and related activities in the country 
through ISRO’s constituent units and major autonomous institutions. DOS is also the nodal 
department for implementation of the on-going National Natural Resources Management 
System (NNRMS). The Organisation chart for Department of Space, ISRO and its major 
establishments are shown in Figure.1

in India
3
Figure 1: Organisation chart of DOS/ISRO
Starting from the sounding rocket experiments in early 1960’s, Indian space science program 
has grown to more complex astronomy and planetary missions. Figure 2 shows the six 
decades of the Indian space science missions at a glance.
Figure 2: The timeline shows the milestones of the six decades of Indian Space Science Mission. 
Courtesy: Nature Review Physics, Das et. al., Nat. Rev. Phy. 3, 722-723 (2021).
Space Science Exploration and Research 
in India
4
The major space science missions of India are briefly mentioned below:
1.4 Achievements in Space Science Program
MARS ORBITER MISSION
Mars Orbiter Mission, the maiden interplanetary mission of ISRO, launched on November 
5, 2013, completed seven years in Martian orbit as on 24th Sep, 2021 and is well beyond 
its designed mission life of six months. MOM data are made available at ISSDC website 
(https://mrbowse.issdc.gov.in/MOMLTA) to registered users. 
Highlights of Science Results 
• 
Enhanced escape of Martian atmosphere during global dust storm (for further details, 
see the inputs in this report as provided by National Atmospheric Research Laboratory, 
Gadanki)
• 
The solar coronal dynamics during the post-maxima phase of the solar cycle 24 using 
S -band radio signals from the MOM (For more details, see the inputs provided in this 
report by Space Physics Laboratory, Thiruvananthapuram) 
1.5 ASTROSAT
AstroSat is India’s first dedicated Space Astronomy Observatory launched into a 650-km, 
6° inclination orbit on September 28, 2015, with a lift-off mass of 1515 kg, by PSLV-C30 
(XL) rocket from Satish Dhawan Space Centre Sriharikota. AstroSat carries a total of five 
scientific payloads enabling imaging, studying temporal and spectral properties of galactic 
and extra-galactic cosmic sources in a wide range of wavelengths on a common platform. 
The unique feature of this observatory is its capability for carrying out broad band simultaneous 
multi-wavelength observation going from far ultra violet to gamma rays. UVIT has the highest 
angular resolution of 1.5 arc sec which is 3 times better than the next best UV telescope 
(GALEX-Galaxy evolution explorer) operational today. LAXPC has the highest collecting 
area in comparison to any other X-ray detector till today. CZTI possesses a unique capability 
of measuring X-ray polarization and also acts as an open detector beyond 100 keV.
Some significant outcomes from the research in the various fields of Astronomy and 
Astrophysics are being carried out at ISRO enabled Indian academic institutions, Tata Institute 
of Fundamental Research (TIFR) Mumbai, Indian Institute of Astrophysics (IIA) Bengaluru, 
Inter University Centre for Astronomy & Astrophysics (IUCAA) Pune and Physical Research 
Laboratory (PRL) Ahmedabad.
Space Science Exploration and Research 
in India
5
Figure 3: Image showing AstroSat spacecraft with various payloads.
AstroSat spacecraft has the following five payloads:
I.	 Ultra Violet Imaging Telescope (UVIT), developed by IIA, consist of two identical 
telescopes of aperture 380 mm. One telescope covers FUV (130–180 nm) band and the 
other covers NUV (200–300 nm) and visible band (320–550 nm). The hyperbolic mirrors 
are super polished.
II.	 Large Area X-ray Proportional Counter (LAXPC), developed by TIFR has three identical 
gas detectors. LAXPC has a total effective area of 8000 cm2.
III.	Cadmium–Zinc–Telluride Imager (CZTI), developed by TIFR works in 20–100 keV. The 
imaging capability is achieved with coded mask. CZTI also has the capability of making 
X-ray polarization measurements.
IV.	Soft X-ray Telescope (SXT), developed by TIFR, uses X-ray reflecting mirrors and an 
X-ray CCD for imaging and spectral studies in 0.3–8 keV. 
V.	 Scanning Sky Monitor (SSM) developed by ISRO is an all sky monitor for detecting 
and monitoring transient sources and for follow-up studies of known X-ray sources in 
2.5–10 keV region. 
AstroSat is operated as a proposal based observatory. The proposals for AstroSat data are 
solicited through anouncement of regular opportunity. The received proposals are reviewed 
by AstroSat Time Allocation Committee (ATAC) and AstroSat Target of Opportunity (TOO) 
supported by AstroSat Technical Committee (ATC). 
Mission operations centre at ISTRAC Bengaluru manages the task of operating AstroSat, as 
celestial objects space observatory in a low inclination Earth orbit and provides all scientific 
data to user community through International Space Science Data Centre (ISSDC).
Space Science Exploration and Research 
in India
6
The task of optimising the spacecraft operations to enable maximum availability of observing 
instruments to seekers of observation is handled through mission operations team.
o	 AstroSat operations consist of complex and elaborate procedures. The spacecraft is 
oriented to a celestial source meeting several safety and operational constraints. While 
pointing and shifting from one target to another avoiding Sun in field of view of sensors. 
Scheduling also considers other constraints like eclipse, south Atlantic anomaly (SAA), 
occultation, earth limb brightness to name a few. Several corrections are carried out on 
regular basis for attitude, on-board timer drift, gyro drift, orbit co-efficients, SAA Entry/
Exit. The spacecraft data is downloaded and the data from the five science payloads 
then sent to respective payload operation centre for validation and subsequently data is 
archived and made available to users.
	
As of April 2022, AstroSat has produced 256 peer reviewed articles in national/ inter-
national refereed journals. In addition, AstroSat data has contributed to 15 theses and 
more than 750 conference proceedings, GCN circulars and Astronomer’s telegrams. 
AstroSat serves 1500+ registered users from 49 countries.
Some of the major interesting discoveries from AstroSat are mentioned below: 
i)	 “India’s ASTROSAT makes rare discovery”, is an exceptional and a welcome headline in 
the history of Indian media for the importance given in recent times to Science, particularly 
space science shared from PTI PUNE, on August 25, 2020. This is the first detection of 
a FUV photons from Lyman Alpha emitting galaxy AUDFs01 at a distance of 9.3 billion 
light years (redshift z=1.42). This observation is made possible due to the high sensitivity 
and low background of the UVIT detectors combined with the long exposure time. The 
importance is well recognised in the international community which has led to a growing 
list of scientists from all over the world joining the AstroSat Ultraviolet Deep Field project, 
as well as initiating a number of new collaborative projects, including the AMUSEDLy 
(AstroSat-MUSE Detection of Lyman continuum sources) project with the European 
Southern Observatory.
ii)	 Deep survey of M31 galaxy, popularly known as Andromeda galaxy with UVIT led to the 
first detection of young main-sequence stars in the bulge of M31 outside the nucleus. 
This survey has produced UVIT point source catalogue of 75,000+ sources in NUV/FUV.
iii)	For the first time, CZTI discovered X-ray polarization from the off-pulse region of Crab 
pulsar. CZTI has also detected polarised prompt emission from gamma ray bursts (GRB) 
in about 20% of CZTI observed GRBs. The results indicate that in a fraction of cases 
the magnetic field in the emitting region is strongly ordered while in the rest the field 
is randomly distributed. These results have spawned multiple theoretical investigations 
worldwide in the radiative properties of GRBs and the planning of space missions 
dedicated to the polarimetry of GRBs.
Space Science Exploration and Research 
in India
7
iv)	AstroSat detection and characterisation of star formation in and around Jellyfish galaxies: 
These galaxies are members of galaxy clusters. AstroSat UVIT observations find that 
new stars are being formed in the outflowing gas streams, away from the confines of 
the galaxies themselves. This is providing major new clues to the gas-gas interaction 
in galaxy clusters and the formation process of stars. Given the importance of these 
observations, AstroSat UVIT has been integrated into the multi-nation GASP (Gas 
stripping phenomena in galaxies) programme. 
v)	 AstroSat UV/X-ray observations of OJ287 shows the importance of simultaneous 
broad-band observations as the FUV data from UVIT leads to strong constraints on the 
contribution of synchrotron component in driving the X-ray spectral changes observed in 
OJ287 over multiple epochs.
vi)	LAXPC and SXT observations of 4U 1630-17 found that the blackhole in the binary is 
rotating at a speed close to the maximum possible speed of spin. 
1.6 INDIAN LUNAR PROGRAM
Indian lunar program began when ISRO launched its first mission to the Moon, Chandrayaan-1 
in 2008. The mission had demonstrated successful insertion into the lunar orbit and 
discovered the presence of water and other volatiles. The mission carried eleven payloads 
from India and 
Major science results of Chandrayaan-1 are as follows:
• The Moon Mineralogy Mapper (M3) instrument discovered evidence of widespread 
surface water. This was further substantiated at the polar regions with the Mini-SAR 
experiment, showing evidence for sub-surface water. Mass spectrometer onboard Moon 
Impact Probe (MIP) showed evidence of water molecules in the lunar exosphere during 
its descent from 100km orbit.
• The SARA experiment provided new evidence for the presence of mini-magnetospheres 
by mapping energetic neutral atoms. It also revealed that solar wind protons are reflected 
from the lunar surface as neutral hydrogen atoms, thus providing a new dimension to 
solar wind – lunar surface interactions.
• Combined analysis of M3, HySI and TMC found large expanses of crystalline feldspar 
which validated the Lunar magma ocean hypothesis.
• Strong evidence for enhanced Na in the plagioclase of the highlands – first direct 
measurement of Sodium by C1XS.
• Digital Elevation Models of many craters of interest and detailed maps of lunar surface 
features including the potential site (buried lava tube) for future human habitability on 
the Moon.
Space Science Exploration and Research 
in India
8
Chandrayaan-2 mission was launched on 22nd July 2019 and inserted into the lunar orbit on 20th 
August 2019. As a followup mission to Chandrayaan-1, Chandrayaan-2 encompasses three 
major mission components of an Orbiter, Lander and rover. While some of the experiments 
on board this mission continue earlier surface and sub-surface mapping investigations 
providing continuity to investigations, some of the International payloads of Chandrayaan-1 
have been improved and indigenised as Indian payloads on this mission. Though the 
soft-landing attempt of lander/ rover was not successful, the orbiter was successfully placed 
in the 100km lunar orbit. 
Unique capabilities of Chandrayaan-2 payloads are:
•	
Highest resolution optical images ever (25 cm) from a lunar orbiter platform.
•	
First full polarimetric measurements of permanently shadowed regions.
•	
Largest surface composition study of Moon using X rays – elemental maps.
•	
High resolution DEM of the lunar surface.
•	
Day-night variations of Argon and other neutrals in the lunar exosphere.
•	
Geotail wake studies at the Moon – particle spectrum and flux.
•	
Mapping minerals in 0.8 to 5.0 micron with a focus on extracting clear signature of 
surface presence of water-ice.
•	
Sustained study of lunar environment using radio occultation studies.
Space Science Exploration and Research 
in India
9
OHRC Image Overview
Zoomed view of OHRC Image

Figure 5: DFSAR L-band image showing Pitiscus T crater
